idiom_name: module-scope instance (one evaluation per resolved module)
implementation_notes: TypeScript inherits JavaScript's module singleton: a file with a top-level import or export is a module, each module is evaluated once and its bindings are shared by every importer, so export const config = loadConfig() is the pattern and a private-constructor class with getInstance() adds runtime boilerplate without adding a guarantee. What TypeScript contributes is the type: export the instance under a readonly interface so consumers cannot assign to it, and keep the mutable state module-private. Where a class shape is genuinely needed, a module-level let behind getConfig() or a class with a private static field has the same single-instance semantics; the type system cannot stop a cast-based second construction.
pitfalls: Uniqueness is per resolved module, as in JavaScript: two copies of the package, a different paths/moduleResolution mapping, or a .ts/.js mix each yield a separate instance.
private constructor is a compile-time check only: new (Config as any)() still produces a second instance at runtime.
Exporting a mutable object creates shared mutable state; type the export as Readonly/ReadonlyMap and keep the mutable state private to the module.
Test runners keep module state for the whole run: jest.resetModules()/vi.resetModules() plus a dynamic import is the only way to obtain a fresh instance.
